Russian forces struck residential buildings and an educational institution in Kharkiv overnight on Thursday, killing at least three people and leaving others potentially trapped under rubble, as a wider assault combining ballistic missiles and drones caused casualties in Kyiv and several other regions.
The attack involved Iskander-M, Zircon and S-400 ballistic missiles alongside 113 Shahed, Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, 76 of them jet-powered.
Ukraine's air defences shot down or neutralised 87 aerial targets.
Two people were killed when a Russian strike hit a residential building in Kharkiv on Thursday morning, while seven people were injured in a Russian missile strike on Kyiv.
A drone also struck a multi-storey building in the city's Novobavarsky district, injuring three people. Local authorities said others may still be under the rubble.
A third person was killed and several wounded in a strike on an educational institution in the city's Kyiv district.
One person was wounded in Dnipropetrovsk region. In Donetsk region, one person was killed and three injured in a strike on a post office in Bylbasivka on Tuesday evening.
Ukrainian drones struck a thermal power plant and a chemical facility in Nevinnomyssk, Stavropol region overnight on Thursday.
The chemical plant, Nevinnomyssky Azot, is part of the EuroChem company and has been attacked at least six times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
The plant produces around 1.42 million tonnes of ammonium nitrate, 1.16 million tonnes of ammonia and 0.17 million tonnes of acetic acid per year. The facility produces components used to make military explosives octogen and hexogen, which go into artillery shells.
The adjacent Nevinnomysskaya GRES power plant, which supplies electricity to the chemical facility among other consumers, was also struck.
Regional authorities in Stavropol said production and energy facilities had been damaged along with a school building and a university branch, and two people were wounded. Schools, universities and colleges in Nevinnomyssk switched to remote learning.
A new fire broke out at the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara region on the morning of Thursday, a day after Ukrainian forces had already struck it and the nearby Syzran plant.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Subkhankulovo pipeline station in Bashkortostan, a major hub in the Transneft trunk oil pipeline system that pumps crude oil from Western Siberia and Tatarstan.
A fire was reported at a plant in Naberezhnye Chelny in Tatarstan; monitoring sources said it may be the Altynpolymer-NCh facility, which processes plastics. Four people were injured in a drone attack in the Krasnodar region. Authorities in Rostov and Voronezh regions also reported air attacks.
Russia's Defence Ministry said 343 Ukrainian drones had been destroyed overnight across 15 regions, over the Azov and Black Seas and over Russian-occupied Crimea. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of servicemen killed in Moscow's ongoing all-out war, returning 250 to the Ukrainian side and 22 to Russia, Russian state news agency RBC reported, citing a State Duma deputy.
The exchange was partially confirmed by Khochu Nayti, a Russian organisation that helps families locate missing, dead and captured servicemen.
"Today, 26 November 2026, with the mediation of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the bodies and remains of 22 Russian servicemen were handed over to Russia as part of repatriation," the organisation said.
The previous such exchange took place on 22 October, when 252 bodies were returned to Ukraine and 25 to Russia.
Similar exchanges have taken place regularly since summer last year, when Russian and Ukrainian representatives reached an agreement in Istanbul.
texts.https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-magsa:
The best MagSafe wallets are compact, slim, and svelte, and they attach securely to your iPhone (or MagSafe-compatible case). They are handy if you only want to carry a few cards, like your work badge or train fare. MagSafe wallets are also great for anyone who wants to travel light and forgo a traditional wallet entirely. We’ve tested dozens, and our favorites are below.
Read our MagSafe guides for more useful accessory recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Accessories , Best MagSafe Power Banks , Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers , and Best MagSafe Grips .
Updated November 2026: I’ve added new wallets to our honorable mentions section and removed discontinued products. I’ve also checked for accuracy throughout.
MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12 , iPhone 13 , iPhone 14 , iPhone 15 , iPhone 16 (excluding the iPhone 16e ), iPhone 17 , iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Duo . It features a hidden ring of magnets on the back of the phone and was developed to create a faster, more precise wireless charging system. Those magnets also connect to accessories such as external batteries, car mounts, and wallets.
If you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it’s also MagSafe (the case will have a ring of magnets inside). This will ensure a proper connection with MagSafe accessories. If you use a non-MagSafe case, the connection will be very weak, and MagSafe products may just slide off your iPhone. We have lots of case recommendations in our guides:
When buying a wallet, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2 connections. The product description should indicate this prominently. Qi2 is the wireless charging standard, and all MagSafe iPhones support Qi2. Android phones now also support Qi2, and some have magnets inside, like the Google Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series (Google calls it Pixelsnap).
MagSafe wallets use the same ring of magnets that lets them snap directly onto the back of the iPhone or a MagSafe- or supported Qi2 case. This gives the wallet a strong and secure hold on your device. The wallets we’ve included in this guide all have the MagSafe seal of approval.
Apple first introduced MagSafe for its iPhones in 2020. The following models support the technology:
To use a MagSafe wallet with an Android phone (or the iPhone 16e ), you’ll need to use a MagSafe case . Several case manufacturers have started adding a ring of magnets to Android phone cases to bring the same magnetic experience native to iPhones.
No, MagSafe will not demagnetize your credit cards. Credit cards have magnetic stripe encoding strong enough to resist demagnetization, and the MagSafe wallets in this guide include a built-in shield designed to keep your cards safe. However, you may run into issues with hotel key cards and some gift cards. Keep those away as a precaution.
I use a MagSafe wallet every day as my primary wallet. I check that it snaps firmly onto the iPhone or MagSafe case—and that it doesn’t slide off when I take my phone out of my pocket, bag, or jacket. I also make sure cards fit well in the sleeve and don’t fall out. I only recommend wallets that feel durable, are easy to use, and can hold the standard amount of cards (at least two to three). I occasionally call on my fellow WIRED reviewers for long-term testing or to check out new models.
UAG’s Metropolis MagSafe wallet is on the spendier side, but you won’t be replacing it in a year or two. It is lightweight yet robust with Kevlar construction. There’s a large slot on the back that can hold up to three cards, and you can unfold the wallet and store an additional three (or cash) inside. It also pulls double duty as a stand if you need to prop up your phone, and you can orient your phone in landscape or portrait mode. — Molly Higgins
Smartish’s MagSafe wallet makes me wish all wallets had a slot on the side to push out the cards. I never had to take it off my phone to access cards. Just give the spacious side opening a little push with your thumb, and the cards slide out. My cards remained secure, and I never had an issue with them falling out. It’s made of vegan leather, and Smartish offers a few fun designs. — Brenda Stolyar
This luxe, super-thin leather MagSafe wallet from Nomad has Apple’s Find My feature built in, so you can easily locate it in the Find My app if it’s misplaced. That does mean you need to charge the wallet, but don’t worry, there's no proprietary cable here. Instead, the wallet can be wirelessly charged on any MagSafe or Qi2 charger; once it’s fully charged, the battery lasts for five months. Easy peasy.
It’s made from vegetable-tanned Horween leather with a polycarbonate frame, and it can hold up to four cards. (A less expensive version that uses Nomad's Camino leather is also available.) It looks classy, and it’s great for anyone with a tendency to lose things. —Molly Higgins
Note that Nomad also sells a dedicated tracker card , which can add Find My to any wallet but will take up valuable space in a MagSafe version.
I love this wallet from Moft, which is compatible with Apple Find My, so you always know where it is. It’s relatively standard-looking, but it has a built-in tripod, which came in handy numerous times when I wanted to film a quick outfit check or take a group photo. It raises your phone camera to 8 inches high, and the wallet is very sturdy, so you can dial in the right angle. It works in landscape or portrait orientation. With space for two cards, it isn’t the roomiest but is rich in features. — Louryn Strampe
You can always rely on Casetify for unique designs. Its Snappy MagSafe wallet is available in various styles and colors. It’s slim, durable, and sleek—the illustrations haven’t faded after months of use. It’s made from vegan leather (aka plastic), but Casetify uses BioVeg , derived from recycled polyester and vegetable oil from non-food and GMO-free corn crops .
It can hold up to three cards, and there’s a built-in shield that protects them from magnetic damage. My only gripe is that it can be a little difficult to pull the cards out when the wallet is attached to your phone or case. I typically have to detach it and use the opening from the back to slide out the cards. — Brenda Stolyar
Ridge’s metal MagSafe wallet feels solid and high-quality. A few of us tested it, and it reliably held our setups, including one tester’s daily carry of eight cards plus a thicker tracking card. The magnets could be stronger, but Ridge does sell a strengthening tray that might be useful if you’re concerned.
This wallet can be a little weird to use at first, but you build up muscle memory quickly. There’s a finger slot for pushing cards out, and you slide them back in on the opposite side. Ridge also includes a Torx screwdriver and extra screws, which are useful for switching out the plates, adding or subtracting room for cards, or adding on accessories like the brand’s wallet chain or cash strap . — Louryn Strampe
Most MagSafe wallets are designed to hold just a few cards, but I love the Moft Snap Field because it can hold so much more. You get plenty of storage space for cards—technically up to eight cards, though more reasonably seven—alongside a dedicated slot for an extra SIM card and a SIM card ejector.
That extra room already puts the Snap Field a step ahead of most other MagSafe wallets, but you can also store just about anything you want inside. It uses a folding design held together by magnets, so you can quickly throw in cash, coins, or paper cards. Regardless of what you store inside, you can easily get to your cards with a pull tab. And, if all of that wasn’t enough, the backing that attaches to your phone can pop out and function as a kickstand. — Jacob Roach
ESR’s MagSafe wallet isn’t bulky, but it also isn’t so thin that it feels insubstantial. It doubles as a kickstand and sticks to my phone reliably. There’s space for five cards—three in the external pockets, plus another two on the inside. I really like the clear window that keeps my ID separate and han…

At least 31 people were killed and 21 others injured when a crash involving a fuel tanker sparked a massive fire on a highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, according to local authorities.
Towering flames lit up the night sky as motorists and pedestrians hurried past the blaze. More than two dozen cars and motorcycles were left charred, the Health Ministry said.
The accident occurred in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Greater Cairo, on the Ring Road, a major highway encircling the capital.

texts.https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2:
Russian forces launch ballistic missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, hitting a shopping centre and other buildings.
At least five people have been killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, a Russian-installed official said, as Russian forces hit Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in a ballistic missile assault.
“Following an enemy drone attack on a parking lot, five people were killed and three others wounded in the locality of Vesioloye,” Moscow-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Russian authorities also reported repelling drone attacks in the Tuymazinsky district in the Bashkortostan region and in the city of Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Russia has claimed the annexation of the southern region of Zaporizhia, which it partially controls, since September 2022.
The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was targeted with ballistic missiles late on Wednesday, striking a shopping centre and two other buildings on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, with warnings for residents to remain in shelters still in place, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Interfax news agency reported.
The Defence Ministry also said Russian forces had struck a dry cargo vessel southeast of Odesa in the Black Sea overnight, according to the news agency. The ministry alleged the ship was carrying military equipment and dual-use goods to Ukraine.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said the residents heard loud ballistic missile impact sounds late on Wednesday, which injured at least seven people.
“People who live in certain areas of the city that come under frequent attack, they go and spend their nights in the shelter, even before air raid sirens raise alarm,” she said. “Coming into this winter, Russia has really heightened its attacks, especially on energy facilities.”
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia “is putting pressure on Kyiv’s military infrastructure, straining its air defences, and everything that can support military supply chains”.
“Russia has also been hitting power plants ahead of cold weather. The aim is to wear down morale and inflict economic damage, in addition to all these military effects,” she added.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, MacAlpine said Ukraine’s energy capacity is below 40 percent of pre-war levels, as a number of the combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and the region have repeatedly gone offline due to attacks.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued on Wednesday after meeting in Florida.
“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added.
The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes after the US leader described Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin.

Egypt has suffered another tragedy as a deadly road explosion kills 31 and injures dozens.
An explosion rocked a highway in Cairo when a fuel truck overturned and caught fire, killing at least 31 people on Wednesday.
Egypt’s public prosecutor has announced an investigation into the crash, and the Ministry of Health said it will continue to monitor the situation.
But Egypt is no stranger to deadly accidents on its roads, despite spending billions of dollars on its transportation systems.
So what exactly caused the explosion and how unsafe are Egypt’s roads?
On Wednesday evening, a fuel tanker travelling on a busy ring road in Giza’s Imbabah district, a highly populated, working-class part of the Greater Cairo area, crashed and exploded, causing a fire that killed at least 31 people and injured 21 others.
Local media have reported that the explosion happened after the truck driver swerved to avoid a high-voltage cable which fell in front of the vehicle.
Twenty-seven vehicles were caught up and burned in the accident, according to Egypt’s judicial office.
Thirty-nine ambulances were dispatched to the scene, taking the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment, the Health Ministry said.
Egypt’s public prosecutor announced that there will be an investigation into the crash and ordered DNA samples from victims.
Egypt, which has a population of around 120m, is known for its dangerous roads. It clocked up a total of 44,940 road deaths and 476,126 injuries between 2019 and 2025, according to the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).
Last year, more than 5,800 road deaths and 84,000 road injuries were recorded by the agency, with pedestrians making up more than one-third of those killed.
Children under the age of 15 made up 1,580 of the deaths and 29,101 of the injured.
A World Bank report in 2020 found that the incidents occur because 97 percent of Cairo’s streets lack traffic lights and 78 percent of them have no clear pedestrian footpaths.
In 2025, there were 170 train incidents recorded, resulting in the deaths of 44 people and injuries to 215.
Earlier this month, at least seven people were killed and more than 125 others injured when a train backed into another, also in Giza, triggering calls for political accountability.
Egypt’s Ministry of Transport said that approximately $37bn was spent on transport investment between 2014 and 2024, but recurring incidents have raised questions about the effectiveness of this project.
The leader of the centrist Reform and Development Party’s parliamentary bloc, Irene Saeed, called for full financial transparency on how the Ministry of Transport spent its funding and loans in 2016.
A member of the Egyptian Parliament and leader of the Justice Party, Abdel Moneim Imam, told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the continued “turning of a blind eye to the shortcomings and the recurrence of accidents without genuine accountability leads to the continuation of the crisis”.

SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine in future?
Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX.
Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit.
Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.
Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.
In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated, and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.
In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026.
According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks.
The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.
HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."
Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.
According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president , the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory.
He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.
Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."
"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.
He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company.
He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."
"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."
SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors.
According to DW sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink.
Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.
But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos.
In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.
Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine.
"Unfortunately , our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.
Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.
When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."

By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?
First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.
Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?
It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.
And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.
Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.
Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.
Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.
Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."
Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria , well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.
Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.
The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.
" Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."
Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.
In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia , despite the risks.
Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."
Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea , the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."
She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.
She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."

The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has sunk off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, and was still partially submerged.
That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface."
The Med Emre sank 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline . It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.
Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.
In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.
While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.
Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.
The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

French actor Gérard ​Depardieu will face trial on charges of raping actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018, his lawyer said on ​Thursday. Depardieu, one of the leading faces of French ​cinema, has denied wrongdoing in the case.
Film star Gérard ​Depardieu , one of the leading faces of French ​cinema, will face trial on charges for alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018, his lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski said on ​Thursday.
Arnould ‌first accused Depardieu of rape ⁠in 2018, saying the assaults occurred in his Paris home on ‌two separate occasions when she was in her ⁠early 20s. Depardieu, 77, has denied wrongdoing in the case, and his legal team ​last year appealed prosecutors' decision for the ‌case to be tried.
However, the Paris appeals court upheld the decision for the case to be ​tried in criminal court. It ruled that Depardieu would be ‌tried for allegedly raping Arnould on August 7 2018, but dismissed a second alleged rape on August 13 2018.
Depardieu – a towering figure in French cinema , who has starred in more than 200 films ‌over five decades, including Green Card, The Last Metro and Cyrano ​de Bergerac – has become one of the most high-profile faces of France's slow-burn reckoning, with sexual abuse by ​some of its most powerful men.
Watch more Gérard Depardieu: The rise and fall of a French film icon
Earlier this month, Depardieu withdrew his appeal against a separate ‌2025 conviction for sexual assault, accepting his guilt and apologising to his victims. The rape trial poses ​a much more serious threat to Depardieu, who could face 15-20 years in jail if he is convicted.
Carine Durrieu Diebolt, a lawyer for Charlotte Arnould, described ​the ruling as a relief for her client.
"She has been waiting for ​this moment for a long time," Durrieu Diebolt said. "She ​is fully prepared for it."
The appeals court said Depardieu could appeal to France's highest court, the Cour ​de Cassation. His lawyer, David-Olivier Kaminski, said they were waiting to see if they would do so.
Legal experts say an appeal to the Cour de Cassation would face major hurdles as the top court only weighs whether the law was ⁠applied correctly, and does not retry the case or re-examine evidence.
Earlier this ⁠month, British comedian Russell Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years after ⁠he ​was convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation
Seven people have been injured - four of them critically - after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, local government officials have said.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
A alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.
The city-run Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said it was treating four "red" cases and three "yellow" - less severe - cases.
On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.
It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Londoner Fred Nathan was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.
"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".
He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.
Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.
"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.
"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."
Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.
Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."
Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.
In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.
In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.
After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".
However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".
Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.
If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

Authorities rescued 17 crew members but one later died in hospital after a diesel tanker sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza. A contingency plan against possible pollution damage is now in place.
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.
The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.
According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.
The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.
The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear.
The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.
Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.
Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.
The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.
The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.
The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.
Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable."
But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood."
"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.
Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

North Korea's leader has toured facilities that produce fissile material and demanded a bigger nuclear arsenal, days after Pyongyang left Donald Trump's offer of a meeting unanswered.
The message, carried by state news agency KCNA on Thursday, is a fresh sign that Kim has no intention of giving up the weapons programme on which his authoritarian rule rests.
According to the state media, Kim visited two nuclear material production plants on Wednesday, one newly opened and the other being expanded. He also toured a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute.
Photos showed him and senior military officers walking past dense rows of what appear to be centrifuges used to make weapons-grade uranium and viewing halls with what were believed to be warheads. Some images were blurred.
Pyongyang did not say where the plants are. It has revealed enrichment sites several times since showing one at Yongbyon to visiting American scholars in 2010.
When it disclosed parts of another site in June, outside experts concluded it was probably a second enrichment facility at Yongbyon.
Kim presented the visit as a response to growing nuclear threats around the Korean Peninsula accusing Washington of encouraging its regional allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and of pledging to share its own nuclear weapons with them.
He described North Korea's status as a nuclear power and its drive to expand the arsenal in both quality and quantity as an "irreversible reality."
He also called for the urgent deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains, citing the danger on the border with South Korea.
Pyongyang has focused on tactical weapons in recent years as hostility with Seoul has deepened.
South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes the remarks on battlefield weapons seriously and remains militarily ready, backed by its alliance with the US.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to analyse the facilities, saying the information is confidential and shared with Washington.
Kim has accelerated the build-up of his nuclear forces since his high-stakes diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019 and has turned towards Cold War-era allies Moscow and Beijing.
Trump again voiced his wish to resume talks while in China last week for the APEC summit, but no meeting took place and Pyongyang did not respond publicly.
Speaking to the New York Post this week, Trump rejected the idea that Kim had ignored him, saying it was "not really the right time" during a busy two days.
He added that he could restart their exchange of letters at any moment, though he admitted they had not written to each other recently.
Kim has previously said he could return to the table if Washington abandons its "hostile policy" and accepts North Korea as a nuclear state. Experts say he is seeking recognition as a nuclear power so that he can demand an end to international sanctions.
Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi said North Korea has been expanding its original enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling it a "serious concern."

Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the next president of the European Central Bank, succeeding Christine Lagarde, EU diplomats have said.
The Spanish economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating rival candidate, Dutch central banker Klaas Knott of the Netherlands.
EU diplomats agreed two other appointments to the ECB’s executive board on Thursday: France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier.
EU leaders discussed the jobs at a summit in Brussels this morning, triggering a formal process to nominate the three policymakers.
EU leaders are bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine , amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.
Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027.
“When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said.
Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan, which would be a painful outcome for member states that are net recipients of EU funds.
Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia , net beneficiaries, want to opt out of the loan. Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico , who has maintained close ties to the Kremlin , has accused Merz of blackmail.
But Merz’s stance has won widespread support, especially among western European, Nordic and Baltic states.
Some governments, however, which support Merz’s goal have reservations about his tactics, fearing the public threat to block cohesion funds could make it harder for recalcitrant governments to climb down.
The discussion on support for Ukraine has become entangled in negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, which will set the bloc’s spending priorities for 2028-2034.
Back to the negotiations in Brussels, European parliament president Roberta Metsola told EU leaders that they cannot expect MEPs to automatically approve a deal on the bloc’s next long-term budget , insisting that parliament’s priorities must be reflected in any agreement.
“Parliament is not a rubber stamp. We will never be, we have never been,” she said at a press conference.
“Let’s see what the (European) Council finds as a landing zone when all the red lines are overcome.”
The final long-term budget must be approved by a majority of MEPs, meaning at least 361 of the European parliament’s 720 members. The vote will come after negotiations between parliament and the European Council, once EU member states have agreed on their position.
On Ukraine , Metsola stressed the importance of continued EU support for Kyiv and its wider implications for European security.
“It’s not only solidarity, it is an investment in the future of Ukraine and our, Europe’s, very own security. The stakes go well beyond Ukraine’s borders, and we must never forget that,” she said.
Turning briefly to Ukraine , president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia is preparing for a “new massive strike” against the country, with energy facilities, logistics infrastructure and essential services expected to be among the targets.
“Unfortunately, the Russians are already completing preparations for a new massive strike,” Zelensky wrote on X .
He said Ukrainian intelligence indicated that the country’s energy infrastructure would again be a primary target, as repair crews continue working around the clock to restore electricity supplies following Russian attacks on “substations, overhead power lines, and the entire power grid”.
Zelensky added that he was awaiting an update from Ukraine’s foreign ministry on discussions with international partners over additional air defence supplies, adding that interceptor missiles for Patriot and Nasams systems were a “key priority”.
His warning comes as EU leaders meet in Brussels to discuss continued financial support for Ukraine, alongside negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget. The European Commission has proposed a further €45bn loan for Kyiv in 2027, but member states remain divided over how the money should be provided , with Germany pushing for the entire bloc to participate ( see post at 9.15am ).

There will also be consultation with experts when laws are implemented to ensure the drafts on both sides of the channel align.

The document includes a caveat that it is “published for information purposes only,” and “may undergo further modifications.” It “will be final upon signature,” it added.

FedEx aircraft sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
Thanksgiving travellers in the US have run into disruption after an incident at one of the nation's busiest airports caused hours-long delays.
On Wednesday, the eve of the holiday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) briefly grounded all flights heading for Miami International Airport, after a FedEx aircraft overran one of the runways.
No injuries were reported, and the FAA is investigating what happened.
It had previously warned that delays across the country would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of severe weather, including heavy rain and wind that are forecast in eastern areas on Thursday.
Early on Thursday morning, tracking site FlightAware reported several hundred delays and cancellations affecting flights within, into or out of the US.
The previous day, it said there had been more than 6,800 delays and more than 160 cancellations.
Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
The incident in Miami prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period on Wednesday evening.
A statement given by FedEx to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".
It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
CBS reported that some Thanksgiving travellers had been delayed by several hours.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport , killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over Thanksgiving, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
The AAA has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the holiday over a seven-day period.
Beyond Miami, some parts of Florida are braced for weather that could cause poor travel conditions on both sides of the US on Thanksgiving Day.
The National Weather Service (NWS) has forecast a strong coastal storm for the East Coast, bringing high winds, heavy rainfall and major coastal flooding.
New York City is among the places expected to be affected. Organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.

Fifa has confirmed it has been the victim of a cyber attack which resulted in personal and business information being stolen.
However, BBC Sport understands the data breach did not include any documents relating to the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, president Gianni Infantino's failed World Cup sell-off plot.
Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt was this week granted access to the files upon condition of signing a non-disclosure agreement.
It is understood not to be a systems or technology failure at the world football governing body, with criminals able to gain access to the documents by impersonating and taking advantage of staff.
"Fifa can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyber-attack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information," Fifa said in a statement.
"Fifa is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.
"Fifa condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data.
"Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned."
Responsibility has been claimed online by a group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club, which last week posted screenshots of Fifa files.
The group claims to have gained access to 12GB of data. Analysis indicates this is less than 0.1% of all data held by Fifa and was targeted at the company rather than individuals.

In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026. Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.
The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.
KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.
North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.
Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South Korea Kim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.
"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.
Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.
"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.
Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.
South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.
Trump still hopes to meet Kim Trump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.
In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."
Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."
Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.
Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."
Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

Norwegian airline says its finances are ‘critical’ and it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term backing
Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and said it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term financing urgently.
The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, announced it was on the brink on Thursday morning, a day after warning that its finances were “critical”.
The airline, like many worldwide, is reeling from surging jet fuel prices that have sent costs skywards since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, as well as hitting consumer confidence.
In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Norse said: “If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board’s ​intention to file for bankruptcy.”
It said it was still looking at options to secure short-term financing and was in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover but said: “There can be no assurance that a viable solution will ​be found.”
Norse was founded in 2021 as it sought to step into the space vacated by Norwegian Air , whose attempts to fly budget long-haul were also abandoned as unviable.
Despite that, Norse revived the transatlantic routes, with a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners and ​many former Norwegian staff.
Norse said in the summer it was exploring a potential sale or merger, and set out on a cost-cutting programme called Project Falcon to save $50m (£38m), including axing about 75 jobs. It also moved its headquarters out of Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia, while the founder and chief executive, Bjørn Tore Larsen, left the airline.
It said it “sincerely apologises to its passengers for the inconvenience caused by this situation”.
UK routes affected include London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town. A winter service from Manchester to Thailand was due to start operating next month.

Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.
In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.
The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Latest figures show difference between number of people arriving and leaving UK was ⁠77,000 in ​year ‌to ‌June
Net migration across the UK has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 with the exclusion of the years of the Covid pandemic.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics and the Home Office show that the difference between people arriving and leaving the UK was ⁠77,000 in ⁠the ​year ‌to ‌June ‌2026.
The ONS figures cover the year ending June 2026, down from an estimated 171,000 in 2025 and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. Annual net migration to the UK in 1997 was 48,000.
UK net migration is also for the first time in the “tens of thousands” since that target was set but never fulfilled by David Cameron’s government in 2010. An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the data published on Thursday.
The 62% fall over the past 12 months – from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025 – results from lower immigration. Net migration has fallen more than 90% since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023.
Immigration fell by 17% over the year to June 2026, driven by fewer non-EU citizens being granted permission to work, study, bring family members to the UK or apply for asylum.
Keir Starmer’s policies last year made care workers and some mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas, suspended family reunion for refugees and toughened restrictions for universities sponsoring international students.
Emigration remained relatively high but fell by 4% (-28,000) compared with the year ending June 2025.
Most people leaving the UK to live in another country were non-citizens who previously migrated for work or study, including those who moved to the UK as part of the “Boriswave” from 2021 onwards when immigration was unusually high.
Reacting to the figures, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said Labour’s policies should be credited for the drop. It will be seen as a boost to Andy Burnham’s plans to keep hold of “red wall” seats in any future general election.
“The Conservatives lost control of our borders. Year upon year, they promised they would bring net migration down to the tens of thousands. Instead, they let it reach close to a million a year, overseeing four decades worth of migration in their last four years alone.
“This government has restored control. Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people,” she said.
The drop has been driven by policies pushed through by Labour and Conservative governments.
Home Office visa data from January to June 2026 shows visa grants to international students fell by 38% (-39,200) and grants to skilled workers including those in the health and care sector and their dependants also dropped by 38% (-26,300) compared with the same period in 2025.
The end of social care visas has caused numbers to fall from 108,000 at their peak to just 1,400 last year.
Migration remains a key political issue, with Labour’s 2024 manifesto promising to reduce net migration, and aiming to “smash the gangs” involved in irregular migration and bringing asylum seekers across the Channel in small boats.
Burnham’s arrival in No 10 has signalled a shift in the way the government views legal migration. Some Labour insiders say that policy is now being driven by economic demands rather than a fear of the riseof Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has suffered a dip in the polls.
The Conservatives claimed their policies under Rishi Sunak’s administration were responsible for the drop, including restrictions on family members that could be brought over by care workers and changes stopping dependants moving to the UK with international students.
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.”
Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said net migration could drop even further next year, and may have a “fiscal cost”.
“We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall.
“Falling net migration is not automatically a problem for the UK economy, especially in the long run. Falling asylum migration is expected to benefit public finances. On the other hand, the number of migrants on skilled work visas has fallen even more over the past year, and that is expected to have a fiscal cost,” he said.
Sunder Katwala, the director of the British Future thinktank, said the figures “will come as a surprise to most of the public” who still tended to believe that immigration was rising. “It must now be time for the political and media debate to catch up and start a new phase of the debate about what happens next,” he said.

Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.
Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.
A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license . Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.
Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible. J Studios/Getty Images hide caption
Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New . He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit .
For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit . Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.
Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms , and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.
